name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q01 - Properties of crystalline and amorphous solids

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Crystalline solids have a sharp melting point and long-range order in the arrangement of their constituent particles.

Statement II: Amorphous solids soften over a range of temperature and are isotropic in nature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Crystalline solids possess a regular, periodically repeating three-dimensional arrangement of constituent particles (long-range order), whereas amorphous solids possess only short-range order.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Claim
Because of uniform long-range order and definite intermolecular forces throughout the crystal, crystalline solids melt abruptly at a sharp, characteristic temperature. Hence, the first claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Claim
Because amorphous solids have disordered arrangements beyond short distances, their bonds break over a range of temperatures, causing gradual softening. Additionally, the lack of long-range order makes the average arrangement equivalent in all directions, so physical properties such as refractive index and electrical conductivity are identical in all directions (isotropic). Hence, the second claim is also correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q02 - Electrical conductivity of ionic solids and graphite

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Ionic solids are electrical insulators in the solid state, but conduct electricity in the molten state or in aqueous solution.

Statement II: Graphite is a covalent network solid that is hard and acts as an electrical insulator due to the absence of free electrons.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrical conductivity in solids depends on the mobility of charge carriers (ions or delocalised electrons), while hardness depends on crystal bonding and layered structure.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Claim
In solid ionic crystals, cations and anions are held in fixed positions by strong coulombic forces and cannot move, making them insulators. When melted or dissolved in water, the ions become free to move and conduct electricity. Thus, the first claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Claim
Although graphite is a covalent solid, it is an exception: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to only three neighbours in a planar layer, leaving its fourth valence electron free to move between layers and conduct electricity. Furthermore, weak forces between layers allow them to slide over one another, making graphite soft. Thus, the second claim is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The claim regarding ionic solids is correct, whereas the claim regarding graphite is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q03 - Primitive unit cells and monoclinic crystal system

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A primitive unit cell contains constituent particles at all corners as well as at the centre of each face.

Statement II: The monoclinic crystal system has all three axial angles equal to \(90^\circ\) and exhibits four Bravais lattice variations.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Unit cells are classified into primitive and centred unit cells, and the seven crystal systems are defined by axial distances and interaxial angles.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Claim
A primitive unit cell has constituent particles only at the corner positions. A unit cell with particles at the corners and at the centre of each face is a face-centred unit cell, not a primitive unit cell. Hence, the first claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Claim
In the monoclinic crystal system, \(a \neq b \neq c\), \(\alpha = \gamma = 90^\circ\), and \(\beta \neq 90^\circ\), and it has only two Bravais lattice variations (primitive and end-centred). It is the orthorhombic system that has all angles equal to \(90^\circ\) and four Bravais lattice variations. Hence, the second claim is also incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q04 - Stacking pattern and void counts in close packing

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a cubic close-packed (ccp) structure, the stacking pattern of two-dimensional hexagonal close-packed layers is \(\text{ABAB}\ldots\).

Statement II: For \(N\) close-packed spheres in either hcp or ccp, the number of octahedral voids generated is \(N\) and the number of tetrahedral voids generated is \(2N\).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Three-dimensional close-packed structures (hcp and ccp) are built by stacking two-dimensional hexagonal close-packed layers, generating octahedral and tetrahedral voids between layers.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Claim
Covering tetrahedral voids of the second layer aligns the third layer with the first, giving the \(\text{ABAB}\ldots\) pattern of hexagonal close packing (hcp). Covering octahedral voids places the third layer in a new orientation C, giving the \(\text{ABCABC}\ldots\) pattern of cubic close packing (ccp). Therefore, describing ccp as \(\text{ABAB}\ldots\) is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Claim
In both hcp and ccp lattices, if the number of close-packed spheres is \(N\), exactly \(N\) octahedral voids and \(2N\) tetrahedral voids are generated. Thus, the second claim is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The claim regarding the ccp stacking pattern is incorrect, whereas the claim regarding void counts is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q05 - Packing efficiency in bcc and simple cubic unit cells

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The packing efficiency of a body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell is \(68\%\), leaving \(32\%\) of the total space vacant.

Statement II: In a simple cubic lattice, the edge length \(a\) and atomic radius \(r\) satisfy \(a = 2r\), resulting in a packing efficiency of \(52.4\%\).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We evaluate the packing efficiency and geometry of bcc and simple cubic unit cells.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Atoms are treated as identical hard spheres of radius \(r\) touching along the body diagonal in bcc and along the cube edge in simple cubic.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Packing efficiency} = \frac{z \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{a^3} \times 100\%\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For bcc (\(z = 2\), \(a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\)):
\[\text{Packing efficiency} = \frac{2 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{\left(\frac{4r}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3} \times 100\% = \frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{8} \times 100\% \approx 68\%\]
Vacant space \(= 100\% - 68\% = 32\%\). Thus, the first claim is correct.
For simple cubic (\(z = 1\), \(a = 2r\)):
\[\text{Packing efficiency} = \frac{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{(2r)^3} \times 100\% = \frac{\pi}{6} \times 100\% \approx 52.36\% = 52.4\%\]
Thus, the second claim is also correct.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both statements are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q06 - Frenkel defect density effect and AgBr defects

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Frenkel defect is a dislocation defect that does not alter the density of an ionic solid.

Statement II: Silver bromide (\(\mathrm{AgBr}\)) exhibits only Schottky defect and never shows Frenkel defect.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stoichiometric defects in ionic solids occur as Frenkel defects (dislocation of a smaller ion to an interstitial site) and Schottky defects (equal numbers of missing cations and anions).

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Claim
In a Frenkel defect, the smaller ion (usually cation) shifts from its normal lattice site to an interstitial site within the same crystal. Because no ions leave the crystal, mass and volume remain unchanged, so the density does not change. Thus, the first claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Claim
Silver bromide (\(\mathrm{AgBr}\)) is a notable ionic crystal that exhibits both Frenkel and Schottky defects, rather than only Schottky defect. Thus, the second claim is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The claim regarding Frenkel defect is correct, whereas the claim regarding \(\mathrm{AgBr}\) is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q07 - Impurity defect in SrCl2 doped NaCl and metal deficiency in Fe0.95O

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) containing a small amount of \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\) is crystallised, each \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ion replaces one \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) ion without creating any cation vacancies.

Statement II: In non-stoichiometric \(\mathrm{Fe}_{0.95}\mathrm{O}\), some \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) cations are missing and electrical neutrality is maintained by the presence of the required number of \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) ions.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionic crystals must maintain overall electrical neutrality when aliovalent impurities are introduced or when metal deficiency occurs.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Claim
When \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\) is added to \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), each divalent \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ion must replace two \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) ions to preserve charge balance (\(+2 = 2 \times (+1)\)). The \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ion occupies one \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) site while the second site remains vacant, producing one cation vacancy per \(\mathrm{Sr}^{2+}\) ion. Therefore, claiming no vacancies are created is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Claim
\(\mathrm{Fe}_{0.95}\mathrm{O}\) exhibits a metal deficiency defect in which some \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) ions are absent from the lattice, and the resulting deficit in positive charge is compensated by oxidising twice as many \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) ions to \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\) ions. Therefore, the second claim is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The claim regarding \(\mathrm{SrCl}_2\)-doped \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is incorrect, whereas the claim regarding \(\mathrm{Fe}_{0.95}\mathrm{O}\) is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SOLIDSTATE_Q08 - Doping silicon with group 13 and antiferromagnetism in MnO

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Doping pure silicon with a group \(13\) element such as boron produces an \(n\)-type semiconductor in which conduction occurs through delocalised extra electrons.

Statement II: Antiferromagnetic substances such as \(\mathrm{MnO}\) have all magnetic domains aligned parallel in the same direction, making them ideal permanent magnets.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Extrinsic semiconductors are formed by doping group \(14\) elements with electron-rich (group \(15\)) or electron-deficient (group \(13\)) impurities, while magnetic ordering in solids depends on domain alignment.

Step 2: Evaluation of the First Claim
Boron (group \(13\)) has only \(3\) valence electrons compared to \(4\) in silicon. Substituting silicon with boron leaves a missing electron (an electron hole), producing a \(p\)-type semiconductor rather than an \(n\)-type semiconductor. Thus, the first claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Second Claim
In antiferromagnetic substances like \(\mathrm{MnO}\), magnetic domains are aligned in equal and opposite directions, cancelling out each other's magnetic moments. It is ferromagnetic substances (such as \(\mathrm{Fe}\), \(\mathrm{Co}\), \(\mathrm{Ni}\), \(\mathrm{Gd}\), \(\mathrm{CrO}_2\)) that have domains aligned in the same direction and form permanent magnets. Thus, the second claim is also incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both statements are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
